Our findings suggest that LLMs internalize deeply integrated representations of high-order concepts, and provide a novel, robust mechanistic path for the regulation of complex AI behaviors.

papers.title: SplInterp: Improving our Understanding and Training of Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we improve the theoretical understanding and training of sparse autoencoders (SAEs) using spline theory?
papers.core_contribution: The paper applies spline theory to understand SAEs, showing they are piecewise affine splines that generalize k-means autoencoders, and introduces the PAM-SGD training algorithm which improves sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.conclusion: The spline theory lens provides insight into SAEs, and PAM-SGD is a promising training method with advantages in sample efficiency and sparsity.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs are piecewise affine splines, and TopK SAEs correspond to Kth-order power diagrams.
SAEs generalize k-means autoencoders but sacrifice accuracy for interpretability compared to the optimal piecewise affine autoencoder (which combines k-means with local PCA).
The proposed PAM-SGD algorithm for training SAEs has solid theoretical foundations and shows promising empirical results, especially in low-data regimes and improved sparsity.
papers.limitation:
The spline geometry characterization is currently limited to TopK SAEs.
The bridge between SAEs and PCA-based autoencoders sets aside the matter of shared decoding vectors.
PAM-SGD makes approximations that break assumptions of the theory and had some empirical limitations (e.g., instability with TopK in LLM experiments).
future_direction: Extending the spline geometry characterization beyond TopK SAEs.
Exploring the incorporation of geometry into SAE training.
Studying the optimal autoencoding with shared decoding vectors and understanding more deeply the pros and cons of PAM-SGD.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have received considerable recent attention as tools for mechanistic interpretability, showing success at extracting interpretable features even from very large LLMs. However, this research has been largely empirical, and there have been recent doubts about the true utility of SAEs. In this work, we seek to enhance the theoretical understanding of SAEs, using the spline theory of deep learning. By situating SAEs in this framework: we discover that SAEs generalise ``$k$-means autoencoders'' to be piecewise affine, but sacrifice accuracy for interpretability vs. the optimal ``$k$-means-esque plus local principal component analysis (PCA)'' piecewise affine autoencoder. We characterise the underlying geometry of (TopK) SAEs using power diagrams. And we develop a novel proximal alternating method SGD (PAM-SGD) algorithm for training SAEs, with both solid theoretical foundations and promising empirical results in MNIST and LLM experiments, particularly in sample efficiency and (in the LLM setting) improved sparsity of codes. All code is available at: https://github.com/splInterp2025/splInterp

papers.title: Variational Sparse Coding
papers.research_question: How can we achieve unsupervised discovery of interpretable features and controllable generation in high-dimensional data using sparse coding within variational autoencoders?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Variational Sparse Coding (VSC) model, a variational autoencoder with a spike and slab prior, which achieves superior unsupervised feature disentanglement and enables controllable generation when the number of true sources of variation is unknown and attributes appear in different combinations.
papers.conclusion: The VSC model retrieves non-linear sparse representations of data, capable of disentangling sources of variation where attributes can be present or absent in different combinations and the total number of factors is unknown a priori.
papers.key_findings:
VSC outperforms standard β-VAE and β-TCVAE in feature disentanglement on data where the number of true sources is unknown and objects display different combinations of attributes.
VSC recovers sparse latent representations that capture both discrete and continuous sources of variation in data.
The model enables unsupervised conditional generation, feature interpolation, and investigation of feature relationships between objects.
A closed-form expression for the KL divergence between spike and slab distributions and a spike variable warm-up training strategy are key contributions for efficient model training.
VSC maintains strong disentanglement properties even when the latent dimensionality is much larger than the number of true generating features.
papers.limitation: The model suffers from posterior collapse during training, where some latent variables become inactive.
papers.abstract: Unsupervised discovery of interpretable features and controllable generation with highdimensional data are currently major challenges in machine learning, with applications in data visualisation, clustering and artificial data synthesis. We propose a model based on variational auto-encoders (VAEs) in which interpretation is induced through latent space sparsity with a mixture of Spike and Slab distributions as prior. We derive an evidence lower bound for this model and propose a specific training method for recovering disentangled features as sparse elements in latent vectors. In our experiments, we demonstrate superior disentanglement performance to standard VAE approaches when an estimate of the number of true sources of variation is not available and objects display different combinations of attributes. Furthermore, the new model provides unique capabilities, such as recovering feature exploitation, synthesising samples that share attributes with a given input object and controlling both discrete and continuous features upon generation.

papers.title: SOSAE: Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder
papers.research_question: How can the dimensionality of an autoencoder's feature space be dynamically and optimally adapted without extensive hyperparameter tuning?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SOSAE, a self-organizing sparse autoencoder that uses a novel push regularization to dynamically optimize the size of feature representations during training, achieving efficient compression and feature extraction.
papers.conclusion: SOSAE effectively optimizes feature representation size via push regularization, significantly reducing computational and memory costs while maintaining model performance across various image datasets.
papers.key_findings:
SOSAE compresses input into significantly smaller feature lengths (3.1 to 4.3 times more compression) than baseline autoencoders while maintaining or improving classification accuracy.
SOSAE reduces FLOPs usage by 23.3% to 32% and memory usage significantly compared to baselines, due to structured sparsity and truncation of non-active neurons.
The feature vectors generated by SOSAE are robust to truncation; removing trailing dimensions does not cause information loss, unlike other sparse autoencoder variants.
SOSAE achieves optimal hidden layer dimensionality with up to 130 times fewer FLOPs than grid search and 34 times fewer than random search for hyperparameter tuning.
SOSAE demonstrates better denoising performance and robustness against zero-masking and Gaussian noise compared to Denoising Autoencoders, while using shorter feature representations.
papers.abstract: The process of tuning the size of the hidden layers for autoencoders has the benefit of providing optimally compressed representations for the input data. However, such hyper-parameter tuning process would take a lot of computation and time effort with grid search as the default option. In this paper, we introduce the Self-Organization Regularization for Autoencoders that dynamically adapts the dimensionality of the feature space to the optimal size. Inspired by physics concepts, Self-Organizing Sparse AutoEncoder (SOSAE) induces sparsity in feature space in a structured way that permits the truncation of the non-active part of the feature vector without any loss of information. This is done by penalizing the autoencoder based on the magnitude and the positional index of the feature vector dimensions, which during training constricts the feature space in both terms. Extensive experiments on various datasets show that our SOSAE can tune the feature space dimensionality up to 130 times lesser Floating-point Operations (FLOPs) than other baselines while maintaining the same quality of tuning and performance.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: SAE-SSV: Supervised Steering in Sparse Representation Spaces for Reliable Control of Language Models
papers.research_question: How can we reliably control large language model behavior in open-ended generation settings by using supervised steering in sparse, interpretable representation spaces?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a supervised steering framework (SAE-SSV) that constrains interventions to a sparse, task-relevant latent subspace identified via labeled data and sparse autoencoders, enabling more targeted control and better preservation of generation quality.
papers.conclusion: SAE-SSV enables effective LLM steering by operating in sparse, task-specific subspaces, outperforming existing methods and providing a more targeted and interpretable approach to behavior control.
papers.key_findings:
SAE-SSV consistently outperforms baseline steering methods (CAA, RePe, Top PC, ITI) in steering success rate across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity tasks.
A notably small subspace of SAE latent dimensions is sufficient for effective steering, enabling targeted and interpretable interventions.
Steering in the structured SAE subspace preserves or improves generation quality (lexical diversity, entropy) compared to baselines, which often degrade it.
The method generalizes to unseen datasets within the same task domain, capturing both semantic directions and stylistic patterns.
The top SAE features used for steering are interpretable and correspond to semantically meaningful concepts related to the target attribute.
papers.limitation:
Requires access to pretrained sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which may not be available for all models or domains.
Only evaluated on LLMs with up to 9B parameters; scaling to larger models is future work.
Evaluation focused on open-ended generation tasks with limited human evaluation; generalizability to more specialized domains remains to be explored.
future_direction: Achieve universal and style-invariant SSVs that generalize across datasets, tasks, and model families by curating diverse training corpora and developing objectives that encourage semantic steering while minimizing stylistic sensitivity.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive capabilities in natural language understanding and generation, but controlling their behavior reliably remains challenging, especially in open-ended generation settings. This paper introduces a novel supervised steering approach that operates in sparse, interpretable representation spaces. We employ sparse autoencoders (SAEs) to obtain sparse latent representations that aim to disentangle semantic attributes from model activations. Then we train linear classifiers to identify a small subspace of task-relevant dimensions in latent representations. Finally, we learn supervised steering vectors constrained to this subspace, optimized to align with target behaviors. Experiments across sentiment, truthfulness, and political polarity steering tasks with multiple LLMs demonstrate that our supervised steering vectors achieve higher success rates with minimal degradation in generation quality compared to existing methods. Further analysis reveals that a notably small subspace is sufficient for effective steering, enabling more targeted and interpretable interventions. Our implementation is publicly available at https://github.com/Ineedanamehere/SAE-SSV.

papers.title: Teach Old SAEs New Domain Tricks with Boosting
papers.research_question: How can we address feature blindness in Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) for domain-specific interpretability without requiring complete retraining?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE Boost, a residual learning approach that trains a secondary SAE to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, enabling selective enhancement of interpretability for specialized domains without full retraining.
papers.conclusion: SAE Boost addresses feature blindness in SAEs, enabling selective domain enhancement without modifying the base model, and represents an important step forward in targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.
papers.key_findings:
SAE Boost significantly improves explained variance and LLM cross-entropy on domain-specific texts compared to a pretrained SAE alone.
The method maintains general domain performance with minimal degradation, confirming it learns complementary features.
SAE Boost captures domain-specific features that general-purpose SAEs miss, as shown by interpretability analysis and lower cosine similarity to base features.
The approach is modular, allowing multiple domain-specific residual SAEs to be applied simultaneously without compromising performance.
SAE Boost outperforms alternative domain adaptation methods like Extended SAE and SAE Stitching in balancing domain performance, general performance, and sparsity.
papers.limitation:
Undertraining the residual SAE (e.g., on fewer than 100M tokens) can degrade general domain performance by up to 31% in explained variance.
Early stopping based solely on domain-specific metrics may lead to suboptimal feature quality.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders have emerged as powerful tools for interpreting the internal representations of Large Language Models, yet they often fail to capture domain-specific features not prevalent in their training corpora. This paper introduces a residual learning approach that addresses this feature blindness without requiring complete retraining. We propose training a secondary SAE specifically to model the reconstruction error of a pretrained SAE on domain-specific texts, effectively capturing features missed by the primary model. By summing the outputs of both models during inference, we demonstrate significant improvements in both LLM cross-entropy and explained variance metrics across multiple specialized domains. Our experiments show that this method efficiently incorporates new domain knowledge into existing SAEs while maintaining their performance on general tasks. This approach enables researchers to selectively enhance SAE interpretability for specific domains of interest, opening new possibilities for targeted mechanistic interpretability of LLMs.

papers.title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
papers.research_question: Do Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) learn meaningful feature decompositions of neural network activations, or can their performance be matched by random baselines?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) fail to reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms, as they recover very few ground-truth features in synthetic experiments and are matched in performance by simple random baselines on real model activations.
papers.conclusion: Current SAE evaluation practices are insufficient, and SAEs in their present state do not reliably learn meaningful feature decompositions. The proposed random baselines serve as simple sanity checks for future work.
papers.key_findings:
In synthetic experiments with known ground-truth features, SAEs recover only 9% of true features despite achieving 71% explained variance, showing a disconnect between reconstruction and feature recovery.
Three random baselines (Frozen Decoder, Soft-Frozen Decoder, Frozen Encoder) match fully-trained SAEs across key evaluation metrics: interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72).
In the synthetic variable probability setting, SAEs recover only the highest-frequency ground-truth features, leaving over 90% of the feature dictionary unmatched.
The reconstruction objective is a poor proxy for meaningful decomposition, as SAEs can achieve strong reconstruction without aligning with true features.
The competitive performance of frozen baselines suggests SAEs may operate in a 'lazy training' regime, achieving most gains through minimal adjustments to randomly initialized components.
papers.limitation:
The synthetic experiment assumes independent feature activations, omitting correlations that likely exist in real neural networks.
The work focuses on standard SAE architectures and does not evaluate related approaches such as transcoders or crosscoders.
future_direction: Explore objectives that more directly incentivize feature alignment rather than just reconstruction.
Design appropriate randomization baselines for related methods like transcoders and crosscoders.
Incorporate more realistic feature dependencies in synthetic evaluation setups.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for interpreting neural networks by decomposing their activations into sparse sets of human-interpretable features. Recent work has introduced multiple SAE variants and successfully scaled them to frontier models. Despite much excitement, a growing number of negative results in downstream tasks casts doubt on whether SAEs recover meaningful features. To directly investigate this, we perform two complementary evaluations. On a synthetic setup with known ground-truth features, we demonstrate that SAEs recover only $9\%$ of true features despite achieving $71\%$ explained variance, showing that they fail at their core task even when reconstruction is strong. To evaluate SAEs on real activations, we introduce three baselines that constrain SAE feature directions or their activation patterns to random values. Through extensive experiments across multiple SAE architectures, we show that our baselines match fully-trained SAEs in interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72). Together, these results suggest that SAEs in their current state do not reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms.

papers.title: Sparse autoencoders reveal selective remapping of visual concepts during adaptation
papers.research_question: How do prompt-based adaptation techniques change the association of model inputs to interpretable concepts in CLIP, and does adaptation activate new concepts or reuse existing ones?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces PatchSAE, a sparse autoencoder for vision transformers that provides spatial attribution of interpretable concepts, and finds that prompt-based adaptation improves performance primarily by adding new mappings between existing concepts and downstream classes, rather than activating new concepts.
papers.conclusion: PatchSAE is an effective tool for interpreting vision transformers, and prompt-based adaptation methods like MaPLe work by remapping existing visual concepts to new class labels rather than learning fundamentally new concepts.
papers.key_findings:
PatchSAE identifies diverse interpretable concepts (from simple visual patterns to high-level semantics) and provides spatial attribution of these concepts in images.
SAE latents contain class discriminative information, as ablating top-activating latents per class significantly reduces classification accuracy.
Prompt-based adaptation (MaPLe) and the original CLIP model activate a highly overlapping set of SAE latents, indicating similar concepts are recognized.
The performance gain from adaptation stems from tailoring the mapping between commonly activated concepts and downstream task classes, not from firing additional class-discriminative concepts.
PatchSAE trained on CLIP generalizes to the adapted model MaPLe, allowing comparison in a shared latent space.
papers.limitation: The scope of this work focuses on the CLIP vision encoder. Analysis of different vision encoders and joint analysis of multimodality could provide more comprehensive understanding.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to different vision encoders.
Jointly analyzing the multimodality of vision-language models.
papers.abstract: Adapting foundation models for specific purposes has become a standard approach to build machine learning systems for downstream applications. Yet, it is an open question which mechanisms take place during adaptation. Here we develop a new Sparse Autoencoder (SAE) for the CLIP vision transformer, named PatchSAE, to extract interpretable concepts at granular levels (e.g., shape, color, or semantics of an object) and their patch-wise spatial attributions. We explore how these concepts influence the model output in downstream image classification tasks and investigate how recent state-of-the-art prompt-based adaptation techniques change the association of model inputs to these concepts. While activations of concepts slightly change between adapted and non-adapted models, we find that the majority of gains on common adaptation tasks can be explained with the existing concepts already present in the non-adapted foundation model. This work provides a concrete framework to train and use SAEs for Vision Transformers and provides insights into explaining adaptation mechanisms.

papers.title: Sparse Autoencoders Bridge The Deep Learning Model and The Brain
papers.research_question: Can we design a more direct and downstream-task-free alignment between model and brain representations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-BrainMap, a framework that uses sparse autoencoders to directly align deep learning visual model representations with voxel-level fMRI responses, establishing a direct, downstream-task-free bridge between DNNs and the human visual cortex.
papers.conclusion: Sparse autoencoders bridge the gap between deep learning visual models and the human ventral visual pathway, revealing high similarity between SAE units and voxel fMRI signals, functional alignment, and hierarchical correspondence.
papers.key_findings:
Strong activation similarity exists between SAE units and cortical voxels, with maximum cosine similarity up to 0.76.
SAE units preserve the functional structure of predefined brain ROIs and exhibit ROI-consistent selectivity.
A fine-grained hierarchical mapping is established between model layers and the human ventral visual pathway.
Visualization reveals that in ViT-B/16 CLIP, early layers use low-level information to generate high-level semantics, while later layers reconstruct low-level information while integrating high-level semantics.
The framework provides a direct, task-free alignment method that avoids the limitations of previous representation-based and prediction-based approaches.
papers.limitation: The training configuration of SAEs was kept the same across all experiments; the effects of SAE dimension, training methods, epochs, and dataset on Brain-Model alignment were not considered, which may affect results.
papers.abstract: We present SAE-BrainMap, a novel framework that directly aligns deep learning visual model representations with voxel-level fMRI responses using sparse autoencoders (SAEs). First, we train layer-wise SAEs on model activations and compute the correlations between SAE unit activations and cortical fMRI signals elicited by the same natural image stimuli with cosine similarity, revealing strong activation correspondence (maximum similarity up to 0.76). Depending on this alignment, we construct a voxel dictionary by optimally assigning the most similar SAE feature to each voxel, demonstrating that SAE units preserve the functional structure of predefined regions of interest (ROIs) and exhibit ROI-consistent selectivity. Finally, we establish fine-grained hierarchical mapping between model layers and the human ventral visual pathway, also by projecting voxel dictionary activations onto individual cortical surfaces, we visualize the dynamic transformation of the visual information in deep learning models. It is found that ViT-B/16$_{CLIP}$ tends to utilize low-level information to generate high-level semantic information in the early layers and reconstructs the low-dimension information later. Our results establish a direct, downstream-task-free bridge between deep neural networks and human visual cortex, offering new insights into model interpretability.

papers.title: Learning Multi-Level Features with Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we train sparse autoencoders to learn hierarchical features and avoid pathologies like feature absorption and splitting when scaling dictionary size?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Matryoshka Sparse Autoencoders, a hierarchical variant that trains multiple nested dictionaries simultaneously to learn features at different levels of abstraction, reducing feature absorption and splitting.
papers.conclusion: Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical interpretability tasks, enabling training of arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.
papers.key_findings:
Matryoshka SAEs significantly reduce feature absorption and splitting compared to standard SAEs.
Matryoshka SAEs achieve more disentangled latent representations and better performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks.
Matryoshka SAEs maintain or improve downstream task performance with increasing dictionary size, unlike standard SAEs which often degrade.
Matryoshka SAEs exhibit a small trade-off in reconstruction fidelity but learn more meaningful features that result in comparable downstream model loss.
The hierarchical structure forces early latents to capture general concepts and later latents to specialize, preserving interpretable features at multiple scales.
papers.limitation:
Slightly reduced reconstruction performance compared to standard SAEs.
Increased training time due to multiple nested reconstruction objectives.
Reliance on quantitative metrics that may not fully capture human-relevant interpretability.
future_direction: Investigate the human interpretability of Matryoshka SAE latents.
Explore the applicability of Matryoshka SAEs to practical interpretability tasks.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful tool for interpreting neural networks by extracting the concepts represented in their activations. However, choosing the size of the SAE dictionary (i.e. number of learned concepts) creates a tension: as dictionary size increases to capture more relevant concepts, sparsity incentivizes features to be split or absorbed into more specific features, leaving high-level features missing or warped. We introduce Matryoshka SAEs, a novel variant that addresses these issues by simultaneously training multiple nested dictionaries of increasing size, forcing the smaller dictionaries to independently reconstruct the inputs without using the larger dictionaries. This organizes features hierarchically - the smaller dictionaries learn general concepts, while the larger dictionaries learn more specific concepts, without incentive to absorb the high-level features. We train Matryoshka SAEs on Gemma-2-2B and TinyStories and find superior performance on sparse probing and targeted concept erasure tasks, more disentangled concept representations, and reduced feature absorption. While there is a minor tradeoff with reconstruction performance, we believe Matryoshka SAEs are a superior alternative for practical tasks, as they enable training arbitrarily large SAEs while retaining interpretable features at different levels of abstraction.

papers.title: A Comparative Analysis of Sparse Autoencoder and Activation Difference in Language Model Steering
papers.research_question: How can we improve language model steering by selecting the most relevant sparse autoencoder (SAE) features and applying a token-wise decaying steering strategy to avoid degenerate outputs?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a method to select the most relevant SAE feature for steering and introduces a token-wise decaying steering strategy, which improves stability and performance in mathematical reasoning and instruction following tasks.
papers.conclusion: Decaying SAE steering is an effective method for controlling language model behavior, providing a more interpretable alternative to mean activation difference, especially in mathematical reasoning tasks.
papers.key_findings:
SAE steering with a single relevant feature and decaying strategy outperforms constant steering and mean activation difference in math reasoning.
SAE steering can elicit step-by-step mathematical reasoning without few-shot prompts.
In instruction following, SAE steering matches the performance of mean activation difference.
The proposed feature selection method effectively removes redundant SAE features.
Decaying steering avoids degenerate outputs such as repetitive words.
papers.limitation:
The proposed method struggles with word inclusion tasks, as no single SAE feature reliably encodes lexical constraints.
The explanations from Neuronpedia are not guaranteed to be precise.
future_direction: Finer-grained SAE combinations for language proximity cases.
Multilingual-aware alignment strategies for steering.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have recently emerged as a powerful tool for language model steering. Prior work has explored top-k SAE latents for steering, but we observe that many dimensions among the top-k latents capture non-semantic features such as punctuation rather than semantic attributes like instructions. To address this, we propose focusing on a single, most relevant SAE latent (top-1), eliminating redundant features. We further identify a limitation in constant SAE steering, which often produces degenerate outputs such as repetitive single words. To mitigate this, we introduce a token-wise decaying steering strategy, enabling more faithful comparisons with mean activation difference baselines. Empirically, we show that steering an SAE latent associated with reasoning reliably elicits step-by-step mathematical reasoning and enhances inference quality, functionally resembling the effect of appending a guiding token. Our results demonstrate that SAEs outperform mean activation difference methods on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and match their performance on IF-Eval.

papers.title: A PCA-like Autoencoder
papers.research_question: How can we create an autoencoder with a latent space where components are ordered by importance and are statistically independent, similar to PCA but with non-linear transformations?
papers.core_contribution: The paper proposes a novel autoencoder architecture and training algorithm that learns a latent space with components ordered by importance and statistically independent, enabling meaningful interpolation.
papers.conclusion: The PCA Autoencoder learns an interpretable latent space where components are independent and ordered by importance, allowing for meaningful interpolation with respect to data properties.
papers.key_findings:
The PCA Autoencoder learns a latent space where the first component corresponds to the surface area of ellipses, and the second corresponds to the ratio between the two axes.
For ellipses with three parameters (axes and rotation), the PCA Autoencoder learns a first axis for surface area and subsequent axes for axis ratios in different directions, separating geometric attributes.
The standard autoencoder mixes geometric attributes in its latent space, making it less interpretable.
The PCA Autoencoder fails to fully separate attributes for disks with varying radius and grayscale, where the second axis mixes both size and grey-scale.
papers.limitation: The algorithm increases the latent space size by one dimension at each step, which can be problematic for learning representations that require multiple dimensions simultaneously (e.g., object position).
future_direction: Extend the method to more complex data.
Consider increasing the latent space by packets of codes to allow more freedom in learning representations, while finding an efficient way to compute the covariance loss for these packets.
papers.abstract: An autoencoder is a neural network which data projects to and from a lower dimensional latent space, where this data is easier to understand and model. The autoencoder consists of two sub-networks, the encoder and the decoder, which carry out these transformations. The neural network is trained such that the output is as close to the input as possible, the data having gone through an information bottleneck : the latent space. This tool bears significant ressemblance to Principal Component Analysis (PCA), with two main differences. Firstly, the autoencoder is a non-linear transformation, contrary to PCA, which makes the autoencoder more flexible and powerful. Secondly, the axes found by a PCA are orthogonal, and are ordered in terms of the amount of variability which the data presents along these axes. This makes the interpretability of the PCA much greater than that of the autoencoder, which does not have these attributes. Ideally, then, we would like an autoencoder whose latent space consists of independent components, ordered by decreasing importance to the data. In this paper, we propose an algorithm to create such a network. We create an iterative algorithm which progressively increases the size of the latent space, learning a new dimension at each step. Secondly, we propose a covariance loss term to add to the standard autoencoder loss function, as well as a normalisation layer just before the latent space, which encourages the latent space components to be statistically independent. We demonstrate the results of this autoencoder on simple geometric shapes, and find that the algorithm indeed finds a meaningful representation in the latent space. This means that subsequent interpolation in the latent space has meaning with respect to the geometric properties of the images.

papers.title: Deep Learning of Part-Based Representation of Data Using Sparse Autoencoders With Nonnegativity Constraints
papers.research_question: How can nonnegativity constraints in autoencoder training be used to learn part-based representations of data, and does this improve reconstruction and prediction performance?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces a nonnegativity constraint algorithm (NCAE) for training autoencoders that learns part-based, sparse features, improving reconstruction quality and the prediction performance of deep networks.
papers.conclusion: Nonnegativity constraints in autoencoder training enable part-based representation learning, which improves reconstruction and classification performance in deep networks.
papers.key_findings:
Nonnegativity constraints force autoencoders to learn features that capture a part-based representation of data.
NCAE achieves lower reconstruction error and better sparsity in hidden encoding compared to SAE and NMF.
A deep network pre-trained with NCAE achieves better classification accuracy than networks pre-trained with SAE, NNSAE, DAE, and DpAE on several datasets.
The learned features (receptive fields) are more interpretable, representing parts like strokes in digits or facial features.
The method works for both image and text data, extracting semantic features from documents.
papers.abstract: We demonstrate a new deep learning autoencoder network, trained by a nonnegativity constraint algorithm (nonnegativity-constrained autoencoder), that learns features that show part-based representation of data. The learning algorithm is based on constraining negative weights. The performance of the algorithm is assessed based on decomposing data into parts and its prediction performance is tested on three standard image data sets and one text data set. The results indicate that the nonnegativity constraint forces the autoencoder to learn features that amount to a part-based representation of data, while improving sparsity and reconstruction quality in comparison with the traditional sparse autoencoder and nonnegative matrix factorization. It is also shown that this newly acquired representation improves the prediction performance of a deep neural network.

papers.title: SPARC: Concept-Aligned Sparse Autoencoders for Cross-Model and Cross-Modal Interpretability
papers.research_question: How can we learn a single, unified latent space shared across diverse architectures and modalities to enable direct comparison of how different models represent identical concepts?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SPARC, a framework that learns a unified latent space across diverse models and modalities via Global TopK sparsity and cross-reconstruction loss, enabling direct comparison of concept representations and improving concept alignment (Jaccard similarity 0.80 vs 0.22 for prior work).
papers.conclusion: SPARC provides a powerful framework for cross-model and cross-modal interpretability by learning a unified latent space, enabling direct comparison of concept representations and facilitating applications like attribution and retrieval without manual alignment.
papers.key_findings:
SPARC achieves a concept alignment Jaccard similarity of 0.80 on Open Images, more than tripling the alignment compared to USAE (0.22).
Global TopK enforces identical activation patterns across all input streams, eliminating mixed activation patterns and ensuring all neurons are either active across all streams or dead across all streams.
Cross-reconstruction loss provides semantic alignment, ensuring the meaning of activations is transferable between streams.
SPARC enables practical applications like text-guided spatial localization in vision-only models and cross-model/cross-modal retrieval without requiring manual alignment.
SPARC generalizes to ten diverse pretrained models (including vision and language encoders) and maintains positive cross-stream reconstruction scores.
future_direction: Exploring shallow nonlinear mappings (e.g., two-layer MLPs) for encoders and decoders.
papers.abstract: Understanding how different AI models encode the same high-level concepts, such as objects or attributes, remains challenging because each model typically produces its own isolated representation. Existing interpretability methods like Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) produce latent concepts individually for each model, resulting in incompatible concept spaces and limiting cross-model interpretability. To address this, we introduce SPARC (Sparse Autoencoders for Aligned Representation of Concepts), a new framework that learns a single, unified latent space shared across diverse architectures and modalities (e.g., vision models like DINO, and multimodal models like CLIP). SPARC's alignment is enforced through two key innovations: (1) a Global TopK sparsity mechanism, ensuring all input streams activate identical latent dimensions for a given concept; and (2) a Cross-Reconstruction Loss, which explicitly encourages semantic consistency between models. On Open Images, SPARC dramatically improves concept alignment, achieving a Jaccard similarity of 0.80, more than tripling the alignment compared to previous methods. SPARC creates a shared sparse latent space where individual dimensions often correspond to similar high-level concepts across models and modalities, enabling direct comparison of how different architectures represent identical concepts without requiring manual alignment or model-specific analysis. As a consequence of this aligned representation, SPARC also enables practical applications such as text-guided spatial localization in vision-only models and cross-model/cross-modal retrieval. Code and models are available at https://github.com/AtlasAnalyticsLab/SPARC.

papers.title: Evaluating Synthetic Activations composed of SAE Latents in GPT-2
papers.research_question: Do synthetic activations composed of SAE latents behave like real (model-generated) activations in terms of directional sensitivity and activation plateaus? What properties of SAE latents are important for this?
papers.core_contribution: Synthetic activations composed of SAE latents can approximate real activations in directional sensitivity when controlling for sparsity and cosine similarity, but they fail to reproduce activation plateaus, indicating that real activations have additional structure beyond a simple bag of latents.
papers.conclusion: Model-generated activations cannot be explained by simple 'bags of SAE latents'; leveraging statistical and geometric properties of SAE latents helps create synthetic activations more similar to real ones in sensitivity, but these synthetic activations lack the characteristic activation plateaus, suggesting additional latent properties influence model computation.
papers.key_findings:
The 'bag of SAE latents' approach is insufficient to produce synthetic activations that resemble real activations.
Sparsity of the top SAE latent, relative latent activations, and cosine similarity between active latents and the top latent are important for synthetic activations to behave like real activations in sensitivity experiments.
Synthetic activations do not exhibit activation plateaus like real activations do.
SAE reconstructions of real activations behave similarly to real activations, indicating that SAE reconstruction error is not the main cause of the discrepancy.
The model is more sensitive to perturbations towards real activations than random directions, and synthetic-structured activations are more similar to real activations than synthetic-baseline activations in sensitivity experiments.
papers.limitation:
The heuristics for constructing synthetic activations leave room for improvement, as evidenced by the gap between them and model-generated activations, especially for activation plateaus.
The method uses cosine similarity between SAE latents to capture geometric relationships but does not account for latent co-occurrence and other relationships.
The synthetic activations do not match the cosine similarity distribution of SAE latents in model-generated activations closely.
The method leverages information from the base activation to construct synthetic activations (though verified that using a different activation does not change results).
The L2 distance curves exhibit significant variability, impacting the effectiveness of the maximum slope metric; more robust metrics could produce clearer results.
The study focuses solely on one layer of GPT2-small and perturbations confined to the final token position; generalizability to other layers, models, SAEs, and context lengths is not established.
future_direction: Developing better approaches to constructing synthetic activations that perform better in both experimental settings.
Checking for the existence of thresholds below which the model output does not respond to changes in latent activations.
Case studies looking at model sensitivity to perturbations in directions created using interpretable SAE latents and taking context into account.
papers.abstract: Sparse Auto-Encoders (SAEs) are commonly employed in mechanistic interpretability to decompose the residual stream into monosemantic SAE latents. Recent work demonstrates that perturbing a model's activations at an early layer results in a step-function-like change in the model's final layer activations. Furthermore, the model's sensitivity to this perturbation differs between model-generated (real) activations and random activations. In our study, we assess model sensitivity in order to compare real activations to synthetic activations composed of SAE latents. Our findings indicate that synthetic activations closely resemble real activations when we control for the sparsity and cosine similarity of the constituent SAE latents. This suggests that real activations cannot be explained by a simple "bag of SAE latents" lacking internal structure, and instead suggests that SAE latents possess significant geometric and statistical properties. Notably, we observe that our synthetic activations exhibit less pronounced activation plateaus compared to those typically surrounding real activations.

papers.title: Transcoders Beat Sparse Autoencoders for Interpretability
papers.research_question: Do transcoders and skip transcoders produce more interpretable features than sparse autoencoders (SAEs) for interpreting neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Skip transcoders Pareto-dominate SAEs on the tradeoff between reconstruction error and interpretability, and transcoders (including skip transcoders) produce more interpretable features than SAEs.
papers.conclusion: Interpretability researchers should shift their focus from sparse autoencoders trained on the outputs of MLPs to (skip) transcoders.
papers.key_findings:
Skip transcoders achieve lower reconstruction loss with no effect on interpretability compared to transcoders and SAEs.
Transcoders and skip transcoders have higher automated interpretability scores (fuzzing, detection, simulation) than SAEs.
The explanations for transcoder and skip transcoder latents are more accurate across the activation distribution and have a lower false positive rate.
Skip transcoders have lower cross-entropy loss increase when patched into the model compared to SAEs and transcoders.
Sparse probing performance is similar for skip transcoders and SAEs, with skip transcoders winning by a small margin in later layers.
papers.limitation:
Transcoders need to be trained on particular components of the model (usually a feedforward layer) and cannot be trained directly on the residual stream, though this can be mitigated by converting a skip transcoder to a 'residual stream transcoder'.
Feature absorption results are noisy and transcoders do not help improve the feature learning in SAEs the way new architectures do.
future_direction: Future work may illuminate the role of the skip connection by comparing it to a learned or analytically derived affine approximation of the MLP component.
Skip transcoders may be better for reconstructing circuits thanks to their lower reconstruction error, and future work could explore circuit analysis.

Transcoder and skip transcoder features may be used for steering, but benchmarks for unlearning and concept erasure require the latent to contain all information in any given residual stream position, which is not currently supported.
papers.abstract: Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) extract human-interpretable features from deep neural networks by transforming their activations into a sparse, higher dimensional latent space, and then reconstructing the activations from these latents. Transcoders are similar to SAEs, but they are trained to reconstruct the output of a component of a deep network given its input. In this work, we compare the features found by transcoders and SAEs trained on the same model and data, finding that transcoder features are significantly more interpretable. We also propose skip transcoders, which add an affine skip connection to the transcoder architecture, and show that these achieve lower reconstruction loss with no effect on interpretability.

papers.title: Learning Interpretable Features in Audio Latent Spaces via Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How can we interpret audio generative models by mapping their latent representations to human-interpretable acoustic concepts, given the challenges of audio's dense nature and limited automatic feature characterization?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a framework for interpreting audio generative models by training sparse autoencoders on their latent spaces and learning linear mappings from SAE features to discretized acoustic properties (pitch, amplitude, timbre), enabling both controllable manipulation and analysis of the generation process.
papers.conclusion: The presented framework provides a method for interpreting audio generative models by mapping latent representations to acoustic properties via sparse autoencoders and linear probes, enabling both control and a better understanding of music generation.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features naturally align with acoustic properties in a near-linear fashion, enabling controllable audio manipulation via derived control vectors.
Linear probe accuracy reveals a hierarchy of decodability: pitch is most linearly separable, followed by loudness, while timbre remains challenging across models.
Analysis of the DiffRhythm generation process shows pitch converges first, followed by timbre, with loudness converging last, indicating a coarse-to-fine progression.
Different audio latent spaces (continuous VAE vs. discrete codecs) exhibit distinct sparsity characteristics and linear decodability for acoustic properties.
The framework successfully isolates targeted acoustic attribute edits while preserving non-targeted properties in generated audio.
future_direction: Apply the method to other generative architectures such as RAVE, ACE-Step, and AudioLDM.
Train probes for richer audio features including rhythm, harmony, and instrument identity.
Use the interpretable features to directly guide generation behavior during inference for fine-grained control.
papers.abstract: While sparse autoencoders (SAEs) successfully extract interpretable features from language models, applying them to audio generation faces unique challenges: audio's dense nature requires compression that obscures semantic meaning, and automatic feature characterization remains limited. We propose a framework for interpreting audio generative models by mapping their latent representations to human-interpretable acoustic concepts. We train SAEs on audio autoencoder latents, then learn linear mappings from SAE features to discretized acoustic properties (pitch, amplitude, and timbre). This enables both controllable manipulation and analysis of the AI music generation process, revealing how acoustic properties emerge during synthesis. We validate our approach on continuous (DiffRhythm-VAE) and discrete (EnCodec, WavTokenizer) audio latent spaces, and analyze DiffRhythm, a state-of-the-art text-to-music model, to demonstrate how pitch, timbre, and loudness evolve throughout generation. While our work is only done on audio modality, our framework can be extended to interpretable analysis of visual latent space generation models.

papers.title: SAE-RNA: A Sparse Autoencoder Model for Interpreting RNA Language Model Representations
papers.research_question: How and what do RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces SAE-RNA, a sparse autoencoder model that interprets RNA language model representations by discovering sparse features aligned with biological structures and ncRNA families.
papers.conclusion: SAE-RNA provides a method for concept discovery in pretrained RNA LM embeddings, enabling interpretation without retraining and offering features for downstream tasks like feature-aware fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
SAE features localize in structurally meaningful regions such as stems and hairpins.
Features exhibit sequence biases like poly-G/C/A/U tracts that map onto secondary-structure contexts.
Deeper layers transition from diffuse to type-selective activations, with a small subset of channels preferentially firing for specific ncRNA families.
The last layer shows diminished signal, suggesting late-stage representational compression.
Features can be annotated using LLM prompting to align with known biological motifs.
papers.limitation:
Computational constraints restricted the scale of training data used for the SAE models.
SAE training outcomes can vary depending on hyperparameter choices, such as sparsity setting, which may influence the granularity and stability of learned features.
future_direction: Feature-aware fine-tuning with SAE-derived features for downstream RNA tasks.
papers.abstract: Deep learning, particularly with the advancement of Large Language Models, has transformed biomolecular modeling, with protein advances (e.g., ESM) inspiring emerging RNA language models such as RiNALMo. Yet how and what these RNA Language Models internally encode about messenger RNA (mRNA) or non-coding RNA (ncRNA) families remains unclear. We present SAE- RNA, interpretability model that analyzes RiNALMo representations and maps them to known human-level biological features. Our work frames RNA interpretability as concept discovery in pretrained embeddings, without end-to-end retraining, and provides practical tools to probe what RNA LMs may encode about ncRNA families. The model can be extended to close comparisons between RNA groups, and supporting hypothesis generation about previously unrecognized relationships.

papers.title: Discriminative Recurrent Sparse Auto-Encoders
papers.research_question: How does a discriminative recurrent sparse auto-encoder learn hierarchical representations that decompose inputs into prototypes and deformations?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the Discriminative Recurrent Sparse Auto-Encoder (DrSAE) and shows it learns a hierarchical representation where hidden units differentiate into categorical-units (prototypes) and part-units (deformations), corresponding to points and tangent vectors on the data manifold.
papers.conclusion: DrSAEs naturally learn a hierarchical representation within a recurrent network, implementing a deep network with parameter sharing, and decompose inputs into prototypes and deformations along the data manifold.
papers.key_findings:
Hidden units spontaneously differentiate into categorical-units (prototypes) and part-units (deformations) after discriminative fine-tuning.
The learned representation is hierarchical: part-units are driven directly by input, while categorical-unit activity builds up over time through interactions with part-units.
The model achieves excellent classification performance on the MNIST dataset.
The learned prototypes are sharp and resemble representative class instances, not blurry averages.
Part-units perform sparse coding on the residual input after subtracting the contribution of categorical-unit prototypes.
future_direction: Exploring the compatibility of additional regularizations and augmentations (e.g., dropout, convolutional architectures, dataset deformations) with DrSAE.
papers.abstract: We present the discriminative recurrent sparse auto-encoder model, comprising a recurrent encoder of rectified linear units, unrolled for a fixed number of iterations, and connected to two linear decoders that reconstruct the input and predict its supervised classification. Training via backpropagation-through-time initially minimizes an unsupervised sparse reconstruction error; the loss function is then augmented with a discriminative term on the supervised classification. The depth implicit in the temporally-unrolled form allows the system to exhibit all the power of deep networks, while substantially reducing the number of trainable parameters. From an initially unstructured network the hidden units differentiate into categorical-units, each of which represents an input prototype with a well-defined class; and part-units representing deformations of these prototypes. The learned organization of the recurrent encoder is hierarchical: part-units are driven directly by the input, whereas the activity of categorical-units builds up over time through interactions with the part-units. Even using a small number of hidden units per layer, discriminative recurrent sparse auto-encoders achieve excellent performance on MNIST.

papers.title: Interpretability Evals for Dictionary Learning Interpretability Evals Case Study Self-explaining SAE features
papers.research_question: How can we evaluate the interpretability of dictionary learning features, and do new sparse autoencoder (SAE) variants improve interpretability?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces two evaluation methods (Contrastive Eval and Sort eval) for assessing the interpretability of sparse autoencoder features, and uses them to show that non-vanilla SAE variants generally outperform vanilla SAEs.
papers.conclusion: New SAE variants are better than vanilla SAEs, validating the evaluation methods, and further development of interpretability evaluations is needed.
papers.key_findings:
Contrastive Eval and Sort eval provide measures of SAE feature interpretability that correlate with evaluation loss.
Non-vanilla SAE variants (TopK, Gated, Tanh, JumpReLU) perform better than vanilla SAEs on interpretability evals.
The self-explaining method via feature injection works well for early layer features but is less effective for complex concepts and larger models.
Interpretability evals can derisk the adoption of new SAE methods by providing quality metrics.
The evaluations are not comprehensive and measure only a single notion of interpretability.
papers.limitation:
The evals are not comprehensive and only measure a single notion of interpretability, which is nebulous.
The evaluations likely do not have the resolution to distinguish small performance differences between SAE variants.
The self-explaining method succeeds less often on larger models and is sensitive to scale.
future_direction: Creating more and better evaluations for sparse autoencoders.
Using self-explaining techniques as complementary tools in interpretability.
papers.abstract: How can we evaluate the interpretability of dictionary learning features, and do new sparse autoencoder (SAE) variants improve interpretability? Introduces two evaluation methods (Contrastive Eval and Sort eval) for assessing the interpretability of sparse autoencoder features, and uses them to show that non-vanilla SAE variants generally outperform vanilla SAEs. New SAE variants are better than vanilla SAEs, validating the evaluation methods, and further development of interpretability evaluations is needed.

papers.title: Gemma Scope: Open Sparse Autoencoders Everywhere All At Once on Gemma 2
papers.research_question: How can we make sparse autoencoder research more accessible by providing a comprehensive open suite of SAEs trained on Gemma 2 models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces Gemma Scope, a comprehensive open suite of sparse autoencoders trained on Gemma 2 models, to accelerate interpretability research.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that Gemma Scope provides a valuable resource for the interpretability community and hopes it will enable and accelerate downstream research.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs show a sparsity-fidelity trade-off, with wider SAEs providing better fidelity at a given sparsity.
SAEs trained on base models transfer reasonably well to instruction-tuned models, with only a small increase in loss.
Reconstruction loss varies with token position, increasing rapidly for the first few tokens.
SAEs perform better on mathematical data and worse on multilingual data.
Using bfloat16 for inference has negligible impact on SAE performance.
papers.limitation: There is no consensus on reliable metrics for evaluating sparse autoencoder quality.
future_direction: Improving SAEs to capture circular features efficiently.
Using SAEs to improve interpretability techniques like steering vectors.
Investigating how SAEs can be used for circuit analysis in larger models.
papers.abstract: Tom Lieberum, Senthooran Rajamanoharan, Arthur Conmy, Lewis Smith, Nicolas Sonnerat, Vikrant Varma, Janos Kramar, Anca Dragan, Rohin Shah, Neel Nanda. Proceedings of the 7th BlackboxNLP Workshop: Analyzing and Interpreting Neural Networks for NLP. 2024.

papers.title: Do Sparse Autoencoders Identify Reasoning Features in Language Models?
papers.research_question: How reliably do sparse autoencoder (SAE) features, identified via contrastive methods, capture genuine reasoning processes in language models, as opposed to superficial lexical or stylistic correlates?
papers.core_contribution: Sparse autoencoder features identified as 'reasoning features' via contrastive methods are often superficial, triggered by lexical cues or stylistic patterns that co-occur with reasoning, rather than capturing the underlying reasoning process itself.
papers.conclusion: Sparse decompositions can favor low-dimensional correlates that co-occur with reasoning, underscoring the need for falsification when attributing high-level behaviors to individual SAE features.
papers.key_findings:
45–90% of contrastively selected SAE 'reasoning features' are triggered by injecting just a few associated tokens into non-reasoning text.
For remaining context-dependent features, LLM-guided falsification generates non-reasoning false positives and meaning-preserving paraphrases of reasoning traces that suppress activation, decoupling activation from reasoning behavior.
Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers, and reasoning datasets, no features were found that robustly satisfied the criteria for genuine reasoning behavior.
A theoretical analysis shows sparsity in SAE decoding can bias features towards stable low-dimensional correlates (e.g., lexical cues) over high-dimensional within-behavior variation.
Steering candidate features yielded minimal or slightly degraded performance on reasoning benchmarks, indicating activation changes do not imply representation of reasoning computations.
papers.limitation: The study is limited to the specific models, SAEs, and reasoning datasets analyzed; genuine reasoning features might exist in other settings or require different detection methods.
future_direction: Developing better methods for identifying genuine reasoning features that are robust to superficial confounds.
Exploring whether genuine reasoning is represented in a more distributed manner across many features rather than in individual SAE features.
papers.abstract: We investigate whether sparse autoencoders identify genuine reasoning features in large language models. We first present a stylized theoretical analysis showing that sparsity-regularized decoding favors stable low-dimensional correlates over high-dimensional within-reasoning variation, biasing learned features toward token-level cues. Motivated by this analysis, we introduce a falsification-based evaluation framework that combines causal token injection with LLM-guided counterexample generation to distinguish genuine reasoning features from superficial linguistic correlates. Across 22 configurations spanning multiple model families, layers and datasets, we find that contrastively selected reasoning features are highly sensitive to token interventions, with 45%-90% activating when only a few associated tokens are injected into non-reasoning text. For the remaining features, LLM-guided falsification reliably constructs non-reasoning inputs that instantiate the feature's token-level cues and trigger activation, and meaning-preserving paraphrases of top-activating reasoning traces that suppress it. Steering the highest-ranked features yields no improvements on benchmarks. Overall, our results suggest that when low-dimensional token-level patterns are coupled with high-dimensional reasoning processes, the sparsity bias of SAEs systematically favors low-dimensional linguistic patterns that consistently co-occur with reasoning. Code is available at https://github.com/GeorgeMLP/reasoning-probing.

papers.title: CorrSteer: Generation-Time LLM Steering via Correlated Sparse Autoencoder Features
papers.research_question: How can we effectively steer large language models using Sparse Autoencoder features without requiring contrastive datasets or large activation storage?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces CorrSteer, a fully automated pipeline that selects task-relevant Sparse Autoencoder features by correlating generation-time activations with task outcomes, and uses these features to steer model behavior with reduced side effects.
papers.conclusion: CorrSteer establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across diverse language model applications.
papers.key_findings:
CorrSteer improves performance on QA, bias mitigation, and safety benchmarks, e.g., +3.3% on MMLU and +27.2% on HarmBench.
Correlation-based feature selection is effective and scalable, requiring only inference-time activations and no contrastive data.
Multi-layer steering (CorrSteer-A, CorrSteer-P) outperforms single-feature steering, suggesting collaborative circuit effects.
CorrSteer reduces side effects compared to fine-tuning, as measured by the Side Effect Ratio (SER).
Selected features are semantically interpretable and align with task requirements (e.g., refusal features for safety, structured output for multiple-choice).
papers.limitation:
CorrSteer is static and cannot easily adapt to dynamic tasks or separate benign from harmful requests without additional context.
The method may capture spurious correlations rather than causal relationships, especially with limited samples.
future_direction: Extend CorrSteer to dynamic tasks and sequential decision-making.
Improve feature selection to further reduce spurious correlations.
Apply the method to larger models and more complex domains.
papers.abstract: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) can extract interpretable features from large language models (LLMs) without supervision. However, their effectiveness in downstream steering tasks is limited by the requirement for contrastive datasets or large activation storage. To address these limitations, we propose CorrSteer, which selects features by correlating sample correctness with SAE activations from generated tokens at inference time. This approach uses only inference-time activations to extract more relevant features, thereby reducing spurious correlations. It also obtains steering coefficients from average activations, automating the entire pipeline. Our method shows improved task performance on QA, bias mitigation, jailbreaking prevention, and reasoning benchmarks on Gemma-2 2B and LLaMA-3.1 8B, notably achieving a +3.3% improvement in MMLU performance with 4000 samples and a +27.2% improvement in HarmBench with only 108 samples. Selected features demonstrate semantically meaningful patterns aligned with each task's requirements, revealing the underlying capabilities that drive performance. Our work establishes correlation-based selection as an effective and scalable approach for automated SAE steering across language model applications.

papers.title: Closed-Loop Transcription via Convolutional Sparse Coding
papers.research_question: Can we use convolutional sparse coding layers to build invertible deep autoencoding models whose performance can compete with tried-and-tested deep generative models?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that convolutional sparse coding layers can be used to build invertible autoencoders that compete with existing generative models on large-scale datasets, offering benefits like interpretability, stability, and generalizability.
papers.conclusion: The paper concludes that convolutional sparse coding based autoencoders are effective for image generation and offer several advantages over existing methods.
papers.key_findings:
The method achieves good performance on large datasets such as ImageNet-1K, comparable to existing autoencoding and generative methods under fair conditions.
It exhibits better sample-wise alignment and generalizability to unseen datasets (e.g., an autoencoder trained on CIFAR-10 can reconstruct CIFAR-100).
The learned feature representations are more structured, with sparse low-dimensional linear structure amenable for conditional image generation.
The method is more efficient and stable, achieving comparable or better performance with smaller networks, smaller batch sizes, and faster convergence.
It is the first to demonstrate that a concatenation of multiple convolution sparse coding/decoding layers leads to an interpretable and effective autoencoder for large-scale natural image datasets.
papers.limitation: The current implementation remains rather basic and is meant to demonstrate its simplicity; there are many aspects that may be further improved for better performance and image quality.
papers.abstract: Autoencoding has achieved great empirical success as a framework for learning generative models for natural images. Autoencoders often use generic deep networks as the encoder or decoder, which are difficult to interpret, and the learned representations lack clear structure. In this work, we make the explicit assumption that the image distribution is generated from a multi-stage sparse deconvolution. The corresponding inverse map, which we use as an encoder, is a multi-stage convolution sparse coding (CSC), with each stage obtained from unrolling an optimization algorithm for solving the corresponding (convexified) sparse coding program. To avoid computational difficulties in minimizing distributional distance between the real and generated images, we utilize the recent closed-loop transcription (CTRL) framework that optimizes the rate reduction of the learned sparse representations. Conceptually, our method has high-level connections to score-matching methods such as diffusion models. Empirically, our framework demonstrates competitive performance on large-scale datasets, such as ImageNet-1K, compared to existing autoencoding and generative methods under fair conditions. Even with simpler networks and fewer computational resources, our method demonstrates high visual quality in regenerated images. More surprisingly, the learned autoencoder performs well on unseen datasets. Our method enjoys several side benefits, including more structured and interpretable representations, more stable convergence, and scalability to large datasets. Our method is arguably the first to demonstrate that a concatenation of multiple convolution sparse coding/decoding layers leads to an interpretable and effective autoencoder for modeling the distribution of large-scale natural image datasets.

papers.title: Interpreting and Steering LLMs with Mutual Information-based Explanations on Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: How to better explain sparse autoencoder features in LLMs to capture semantic meaning and use these explanations to steer LLM behaviors, particularly for defending against jailbreak attacks.
papers.core_contribution: Proposes a mutual information-based explanation method for sparse autoencoder features that mitigates frequency bias and enables effective steering of LLM behaviors, particularly for enhancing safety against jailbreak attacks.
papers.conclusion: The work demonstrates that discourse-level explanations from sparse autoencoders are crucial for understanding and steering LLM behaviors, particularly for safety applications.
papers.key_findings:
Theoretical analysis reveals frequency bias in sparse autoencoder features between discourse topics and linguistic patterns.
The proposed mutual information-based method generates more discourse-level explanations compared to baseline methods like TopAct and N2G.
The discourse-level explanations are effective in steering LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks.
Experiments show a higher successful explained rate for features with the proposed method.
Steering strategies such as amplification and calibration can enhance LLM safety without additional model training.
papers.limitation: The approach relies on existing sparse autoencoders without modifying their architectures or training to mitigate frequency bias.
future_direction: Designing improved architectures or training objectives for sparse autoencoders to inherently mitigate frequency bias.
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) excel at handling human queries, but they can occasionally generate flawed or unexpected responses. Understanding their internal states is crucial for understanding their successes, diagnosing their failures, and refining their capabilities. Although sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have shown promise for interpreting LLM internal representations, limited research has explored how to better explain SAE features, i.e., understanding the semantic meaning of features learned by SAE. Our theoretical analysis reveals that existing explanation methods suffer from the frequency bias issue, where they emphasize linguistic patterns over semantic concepts, while the latter is more critical to steer LLM behaviors. To address this, we propose using a fixed vocabulary set for feature interpretations and designing a mutual information-based objective, aiming to better capture the semantic meaning behind these features. We further propose two runtime steering strategies that adjust the learned feature activations based on their corresponding explanations. Empirical results show that, compared to baselines, our method provides more discourse-level explanations and effectively steers LLM behaviors to defend against jailbreak attacks. These findings highlight the value of explanations for steering LLM behaviors in downstream applications. We will release our code and data once accepted.

papers.title: Universal Sparse Autoencoders: Interpretable Cross-Model Concept Alignment
papers.research_question: How to discover and align interpretable concepts across multiple pretrained deep neural networks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Universal Sparse Autoencoders (USAEs), a framework that learns a shared, interpretable concept space across multiple models, enabling cross-model analysis and coordinated activation maximization.
papers.conclusion: USAEs provide a practical and powerful tool for multi-model interpretability, shedding light on the commonalities and distinctions that arise when different architectures, tasks, and datasets converge on shared high-level abstractions.
papers.key_findings:
USAEs discover a broad range of universal concepts from low-level features (e.g., colors, textures) to high-level structures (e.g., parts, objects).
There is a strong correlation between concept universality and importance in reconstruction.
DinoV2 encodes unique features (e.g., perspective and depth cues) not found in other vision models.
Universal training discovers shared representations not uncovered in model-specific SAE training.
Coordinated activation maximization enables simultaneous visualization of a universal concept across multiple networks.
papers.limitation:
Sensitivity to hyperparameters when increasing the number of models involved in universal training.
Constrained to discovering features at the last layer of each vision model.
A small percentage of concepts are uninterpretable, possibly due to superposition or being difficult for humans to understand.
future_direction: Exploring universal features across different layer depths.
papers.abstract: We present Universal Sparse Autoencoders (USAEs), a framework for uncovering and aligning interpretable concepts spanning multiple pretrained deep neural networks. Unlike existing concept-based interpretability methods, which focus on a single model, USAEs jointly learn a universal concept space that can reconstruct and interpret the internal activations of multiple models at once. Our core insight is to train a single, overcomplete sparse autoencoder (SAE) that ingests activations from any model and decodes them to approximate the activations of any other model under consideration. By optimizing a shared objective, the learned dictionary captures common factors of variation-concepts-across different tasks, architectures, and datasets. We show that USAEs discover semantically coherent and important universal concepts across vision models; ranging from low-level features (e.g., colors and textures) to higher-level structures (e.g., parts and objects). Overall, USAEs provide a powerful new method for interpretable cross-model analysis and offers novel applications, such as coordinated activation maximization, that open avenues for deeper insights in multi-model AI systems

papers.title: Enhancing LLM Steering through Sparse Autoencoder-Based Vector Refinement
papers.research_question: How can steering vectors for controlling large language models be refined to be effective when only limited training data is available?
